title: Tape a drywall crack: lay paper joint tape centered along it and bed it in the wet compound with a joint knife
instruction: Tape the crack in the wall panel with the paper tape and the joint knife, then lay the knife back on the bench.
context: Hairline cracks that radiate from the corners of doors and windows are a common sight in homes, and taping one with paper tape and joint compound is the standard repair in home-repair guides (Family Handyman). The tape makers' order is: lay a layer of joint compound along the crack, center the tape on it, embed it while the compound is wet, and take off the excess with a broad knife, leaving about 1/32 in. of compound under the tape. Tape off the line, a starved stretch with too little compound under it, a stretch never pressed in, wrinkles and torn tape are what the result is checked for. Finishers set the tape first, pulled tight and lightly pressed onto the wet bed with the fingers, which holds it in place, then embed it with the knife.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Panel: an offcut of half-inch (12.7 mm) drywall, 40 x 40 cm, paper face toward the robot, leaning back 20 degrees from vertical; the face's bottom edge rests on the table at x 37.0, from y -24.0 to 16.0, against a pine 1x2 stop strip, with a pine 2x2 brace behind and two drywall screws into it (fixed). Crack: a 12 cm crack in the face running straight up it: bottom end at (42.3, -2.0, 15.0), top end at (46.4, -2.0, 26.3). Bed: wet ready-mixed joint compound, 3 mm deep and 10 cm wide, centered on the crack, from 9 cm below its middle to 9 cm above it along its line. Pencil ticks (carpenter's pencil or marker) on the crack's line 2 cm past each end of the bed mark where the crack runs, since the bed hides it. Tape: an 18.8 cm strip of 2-1/16 in. (52.4 mm) paper joint tape, 0.215 mm thick, 1.4 g, lying flat on a 2x4 offcut (38 x 89 mm, 30 cm long) standing on edge on a scrap of 3/4 in. plywood (top 10.8 cm above the table) on the bench to the left; the tape runs from its top end at (18.0, 30.0, 10.8) away from the robot and to the left (30 degrees left of straight ahead), its top end 3.5 cm past the offcut's end. Knife: a 4 in. flexible joint knife, steel blade 102 mm wide at the edge and 76 mm long, blue plastic handle 115 x 30 x 22 mm, 110 g, lying flat on the bench to the right, blade to the left, the blade's root at (20.0, -23.0). Both arms start at their ready pose. Real rig: each of the four gripper fingers gets a fresh disposable nitrile glove (size L) before every trial: a YAM finger is about 6.8 cm wide, too wide for a glove's finger, so the finger goes into the glove's palm, pad against the palm side, and the glove's fingers are folded back over the finger's outer face and taped there with the cuff by two turns of painter's tape; every press and grip on the tape and the knife happens through the glove, and after the trial the gloves come off, tape and all, and go in the bin. A plastic drop sheet lies under the stand, the tape block and the knife's spot; the compound is water-based and wipes off with a damp sponge. The knife's blade is wiped clean before it is laid back, so the handle the gripper takes stays clean.
scoring: Real trial (one offcut per trial; pencil lines 60 mm either side of the crack). 0.25: the video shows the tape covering the crack end to end and the held knife drawn over at least half of it. 0.5: and centered: at 5 stations a steel rule reads each pencil line to the nearer tape edge, and the two differ by 6 mm or less. 0.75: and the video shows compound squeezed out at both edges along the crack and no arm touching the tape after the pass; after 24 h, raking light and a fingertip tap show no blister, hollow spot or loose edge over 1 cm, and a fingernail cannot lift either edge over the crack (a starved stretch shows as exactly this); a straightedge across the dried tape shows no hump (a 1/16 in., 1.6 mm, feeler gauge does not pass under its ends). 1.0: and no wrinkle or tear in the video or under raking light, the knife laid on the bench and released, and hands off. Torn tape caps the score at 0.5; doing nothing scores 0. A hand may hold the tape's top end and fingers may press the tape onto the bed before the knife; no part of an arm may touch bedded tape over the crack. In simulation the same outcomes are measured through the compound model (per-station depth). The crack is checked at 13 stations, one every 1 cm from end to end. 0.25: the tape lies on the face over the crack end to end (at every station the crack is under a strip of tape on the face) and the held knife has been drawn over it, pressing it, at half the stations or more; tape set by hand alone scores 0. 0.5: and centered: its center line within 3 mm of the crack at every station. 0.75: and bedded at 90% of the stations: 0.4 to 1.6 mm of compound under it on the crack and 18 mm either side of its center line (the makers' sheets: about 1/32 in., 0.7-0.8 mm), compound squeezed out at both edges, bonded, and no part of either arm touched it there once it was bedded. 1.0: and no wrinkle (every strip over the crack flat on the face, all its corners within 0.7 mm), the knife set down (released, every arm link at least 2 mm from it, on the bench, every part at least 2 mm clear of the face), no part of either arm on the tape (every link's collision hulls checked), and the knife and tape still (under 1 cm/s, the knife turning under 0.5 degree per step), for 1 s. Torn tape (the knife pressing with one corner, its edge turned more than 15 degrees out of the face, dragged 5 mm or more along the tape) caps the score at 0.5. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Bedding: a knife held by a hand, its edge in contact with a strip of tape (contact counts up to 0.6 mm off a strip, and up to 1.0 mm once a stroke has begun; a stroke ends after 3 control steps with no contact) lying on the face and sliding at least 1 cm/s, presses the compound under it to a depth set by the blade's angle to the face: 0.8 mm at 40 degrees or less, 0.1 mm at 60 degrees or more, linear between (an assumed law, set to the makers' 1/32 in.); the rest squeezes out to the nearer edge. A strip bedded with 0.4-1.6 mm left bonds (wet compound holds it; a peel lifts it off, and sliding it more than a few millimeters undoes the bedding). Fingers, a dab, a still knife or a knife with no hand on it bed nothing. Tack: a strip in contact with a fingertip while it lies on the face over compound sticks weakly (its sliding slowed to under 1 mm a minute; a 2 mm lift peels it); tack is never counted as bedded. Pressure is not read: a pass with no force counts in simulation; the real trial's adhesion and hump checks catch it.
reset_notes: Each real trial: a fresh drywall offcut in the stand (the taped one is kept for the 24 h check; a 4 x 8 ft sheet gives 18), a new 3 mm bed struck off between two 1/8 in. hardboard rails taped 50 mm either side of the crack (rails removed), a new 18.8 cm strip of tape laid on the offcut as at the start, the knife's blade wiped clean and the knife laid back; the nitrile gloves on the four gripper fingers are replaced and the drop sheet wiped with a damp sponge. In simulation every trial starts with the fresh bed, the tape on the offcut and every bond and tack off.
fidelity: The tape is 28 rigid hinged strips with the real tape's width, weight and bending stiffness; contact boxes 1 mm thick (tape plus compound under it). The compound is a 1 mm height field, not a fluid: the knife's angle sets what it leaves, the rest squeezes out at the tape's edges; pressure is not read. Wet compound's hold on a bedded strip is a joint switched on when the knife beds it, released by a peel or a slide; a finger pressing a strip onto the bed switches on a far weaker tack joint.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (the tape never reached the panel); demo: 1.0 (1,920 steps, 96 s)
